introduction: This foundational level merges two massive pillars of physical chemistry. It introduces the First Law of Thermodynamics, enthalpy, and the macroscopic rules of Chemical Equilibrium (Law of Mass Action and Le Chatelier's Principle). Mastery of these principles is critical for solving energy and reaction-yield problems.

core_concepts.title: First Law of Thermodynamics & State Functions
core_concepts.description: The law of conservation of energy. The mathematical formulation is $\Delta U = q + w$, where $\Delta U$ is the change in internal energy, $q$ is heat exchanged, and $w$ is work done. State functions (like $U, H, S, G, T, P, V$) depend ONLY on the initial and final states of the system, not the path taken. Path functions (like $q$ and $w$) depend on the specific route taken to reach the final state.

core_concepts.title: Enthalpy ($\Delta H$) and its Relation to Internal Energy
core_concepts.description: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. $\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For chemical reactions involving gases, this transforms into the highly tested equation: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$, where $\Delta n_g$ is the difference in the number of moles of gaseous products and gaseous reactants. If $\Delta H$ is negative, the reaction is Exothermic; if positive, Endothermic.

core_concepts.title: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constants
core_concepts.description: For a reversible reaction $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$ at equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction. The equilibrium constant in terms of concentration is $K_c = \frac{[C]^c [D]^d}{[A]^a [B]^b}$. In terms of partial pressures for gases, it is $K_p = \frac{(p_C)^c (p_D)^d}{(p_A)^a (p_B)^b}$. Pure solids and pure liquids are assigned an active mass of strictly 1 and are excluded from the expression.

core_concepts.title: Relationship between $K_p$ and $K_c$
core_concepts.description:
The fundamental relation connecting the two constants is $K_p = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n_g}$. 
- If $\Delta n_g = 0$ (e.g., $H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI$), then $K_p = K_c$.
- If $\Delta n_g > 0$ (e.g., $PCl_5 \rightleftharpoons PCl_3 + Cl_2$), then $K_p > K_c$.
- If $\Delta n_g < 0$ (e.g., $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$), then $K_p < K_c$.

core_concepts.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
core_concepts.description:
If a dynamic equilibrium is disturbed by changing the conditions (concentration, pressure, volume, or temperature), the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract the change.
- Concentration: Adding reactant shifts equilibrium forward.
- Pressure: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with FEWER gaseous moles.
- Temperature: Increasing temperature favors the ENDOTHERMIC direction.

important_entities.name: Standard Enthalpy of Formation ($\Delta H_f^\circ$)
important_entities.key_fact: The enthalpy change when exactly 1 mole of a compound is formed directly from its constituent elements in their standard reference states.
important_entities.significance: The $\Delta H_f^\circ$ of any element in its most stable, standard state (e.g., $O_2(g)$, $C(\text{graphite})$, $Br_2(l)$) is arbitrarily taken as ZERO. The enthalpy of any reaction can be found using: $\Delta H_{\text{rxn}} = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Reactants})$.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In Chemistry (IUPAC convention), work done ON the system (compression) adds energy to the system, so it is POSITIVE ($+w = -P\Delta V$). Work done BY the system (expansion) is NEGATIVE ($-w$). In Physics, the convention is traditionally the exact opposite. Always use the Chemistry IUPAC convention for Physical Chemistry problems!

Adding an inert gas at CONSTANT VOLUME has absolutely ZERO effect on the equilibrium position because the partial pressures of the reacting gases do not change. Adding inert gas at CONSTANT PRESSURE increases the total volume, shifting the equilibrium toward the side with MORE gaseous moles.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Endo is Direct, Exo is Inverse
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: For Endothermic reactions ($\Delta H > 0$), as Temperature ($T$) increases, the Equilibrium Constant ($K$) also increases (Direct relationship). For Exothermic reactions ($\Delta H < 0$), as $T$ increases, $K$ decreases (Inverse relationship). This is mathematically proven by the van 't Hoff equation.

exam_strategy_tips: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation implies that thermochemical equations can be treated like ordinary algebraic equations. If you reverse a reaction, flip the sign of $\Delta H$. If you multiply a reaction by a coefficient '$n$', multiply $\Delta H$ by '$n$'. For Equilibrium constants, reversing the reaction inverts the constant ($1/K$), and multiplying by '$n$' raises the constant to the power of '$n$' ($K^n$).
